units.title: Unit 47 — Movement and speed
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 98–99 (PDF pages 102–103).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Select fast, quick, rapid, speedy, swift, prompt, brisk and hasty with their natural noun partners, recognising formal and potentially negative meanings.
Describe slow movement, traffic delays and maximum or dangerous speeds using established expressions.
Describe acceleration, changes of direction, detours, balance and lost objects with accurate verb–noun combinations.
Correct frequent collocation errors involving speed, movement and direction.

items.example: A fast car pulled into the driveway.
items.note: Fast describes a vehicle that travels at high speed; quick car is not the usual collocation.

items.example: We took a fast train to Manchester to save time.
items.note: Fast is the natural adjective for a train capable of high speeds, rather than speedy train.

items.example: A delivery van was blocking the fast lane on the motorway.
items.note: In British English, the fast lane informally refers to the lane used by faster traffic; observe local rules on overtaking.

items.example: A fast computer helps when I compile large projects.
items.note: Fast naturally describes a computer with high processing speed.

items.example: The course moves at a fast pace, so review each lesson.
items.note: Pace is the rate at which an activity progresses; a fast pace is demanding.

items.example: Could you take a quick look at this drawing?
items.note: Quick describes a short action; a fast look is unnatural.

items.example: He gave the report a quick glance before the call.
items.note: Glance suggests looking briefly; quick, rather than speedy, is its common modifier.

items.example: I need a quick answer before I confirm the booking.
items.note: Quick refers to how soon the answer is given; a prompt response is a more formal alternative.

items.example: We had to make a quick decision when the road closed.
items.note: Quick stresses speed; hasty can imply inadequate thought.

items.example: I had a quick shower after the morning run.
items.note: Quick, not fast, normally modifies shower when it takes little time.

items.example: We grabbed a quick lunch between the two sessions.
items.note: Quick is natural with meals that do not take long; rapid lunch is not idiomatic.

items.example: Rapid growth put pressure on the town’s transport network.
items.note: Rapid commonly modifies changes in quantity or size and is more formal than fast.

items.example: The survey recorded a rapid decline in local bird numbers.
items.note: Rapid decline describes a swift fall over a relatively short period.

items.example: Rapid change in the industry has created new jobs.
items.note: Rapid commonly combines with abstract processes such as change; slightly more formal than quick.

items.example: The trainees made rapid progress after several practice sessions.
items.note: Make progress is the verb–noun pairing; rapid is a common formal modifier.

items.example: There was a rapid increase in electricity demand during the heatwave.
items.note: Rapid increase commonly describes an upward trend; rapid growth has a related meaning.

items.example: The camera detected rapid movement near the entrance.
items.note: Rapid can modify movement, especially in more technical or formal descriptions.

items.example: Everyone wished her a speedy recovery after the operation.
items.note: Speedy recovery is common in good wishes and has a slightly formal or polite tone.

items.example: The chair hoped for a speedy conclusion to the negotiations.
items.note: Speedy conclusion emphasises finishing promptly, usually in formal settings.

items.example: Thank you for your speedy response to our request.
items.note: Speedy response is a polite and somewhat formal expression, often in correspondence.

items.example: The new portal provides speedy access to the archived files.
items.note: Speedy access highlights how quickly information or a service can be reached.

items.example: The maintenance team took swift action to prevent further damage.
items.note: Take swift action conveys immediate, decisive intervention; swift is relatively formal.

items.example: The company issued a swift response to the complaints.
items.note: Swift emphasises promptness and often conveys decisive action in formal writing.

items.example: The goalkeeper’s swift reaction prevented a goal.
items.note: A swift reaction follows an event without much delay; swift is slightly formal.

items.example: Doctors were encouraged by his swift recovery.
items.note: A relatively formal alternative to speedy recovery.

items.example: The supplier offers a discount for prompt payment.
items.note: Prompt payment means paying without unnecessary delay, sometimes before a due date; common in business contexts.

items.example: I appreciated her prompt reply to my email.
items.note: Prompt stresses not keeping someone waiting; particularly natural in formal messages.

items.example: The support desk provided a prompt response to the incident.
items.note: A common polite or professional expression for a response given without delay.

items.example: We went for a brisk walk before breakfast.
items.note: A brisk walk is energetic and fairly quick, but not a run.

items.example: The guide set a brisk pace along the coastal path.
items.note: Brisk suggests energetic speed and purpose, especially when walking.

items.pt: negócios estão movimentados; movimento comercial está forte
items.example: Business is brisk at the market on Saturday mornings.
items.note: Brisk business means active trading or steady sales, not people rushing around.

items.example: She organised the registration desk with brisk efficiency.
items.note: Brisk efficiency suggests a quick, energetic and businesslike way of working.

items.example: A hasty decision now could create problems later.
items.note: Hasty often criticises action taken without adequate thought, unlike a neutral quick decision.

items.example: He made a hasty exit when he realised he was late.
items.note: Make a hasty exit suggests leaving suddenly or hurriedly, often awkwardly.

items.example: Avoid reaching a hasty conclusion before checking the evidence.
items.note: A hasty conclusion may be based on insufficient thought or evidence, unlike a speedy conclusion.

items.pt: palavras precipitadas; palavras ditas sem pensar
items.example: She regretted her hasty words after the argument.
items.note: Hasty words are said too quickly, often causing offence or regret.

items.example: The manufacturer lists a top speed of 160 kilometres per hour.
items.note: Top speed refers to the maximum speed a vehicle can achieve, not its usual travelling speed.

items.example: The rider sped downhill at breakneck speed.
items.note: An emphatic expression for extremely fast and dangerous movement, often conveying disapproval.

items.example: The replay showed the jump in slow motion.
items.note: The fixed phrase in slow motion describes movement shown at reduced speed; slow movement is not equivalent.

items.pt: trânsito lento; tráfego que anda devagar
items.example: We were delayed by slow-moving traffic near the tunnel.
items.note: A compound modifier describing traffic that continues to move, but only slowly.

items.pt: reduzir a velocidade até quase parar
items.example: Traffic slowed to a crawl when the fog got thicker.
items.note: To slow to a crawl is to move extremely slowly, though not necessarily to stop entirely.

items.example: The assembly line came to a standstill during the power cut.
items.note: A complete stop; unlike slow to a crawl, no movement remains.

items.example: He explained the procedure in an unhurried manner.
items.note: Means slowly and without rushing; the textbook notes that it can sometimes imply mild criticism.

items.pt: café da manhã sem pressa; café da manhã tranquilo
items.example: We enjoyed a leisurely breakfast on Sunday.
items.note: Leisurely suggests relaxed time without pressure; usually positive.

items.example: The download was painfully slow on the hotel Wi-Fi.
items.note: Painfully intensifies slow and expresses frustration or difficulty.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: The cyclist gathered speed on the long descent.
items.note: Means accelerate; pick up speed is a more conversational alternative.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: The boat picked up speed as it entered deeper water.
items.note: A natural alternative to gather speed; this sense of pick up means increase.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: We took a shortcut through the park to reach the station.
items.note: Take is the normal verb with shortcut; a shortcut is a shorter route.

items.pt: fazer um desvio; seguir por um caminho alternativo
items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: We had to make a detour around the flooded bridge.
items.note: Make a detour is a normal pairing for following a different route, often because of an obstacle.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: The driver took a detour to avoid the roadworks.
items.note: An accepted alternative to make a detour; both involve taking an indirect route.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: She lost her balance while standing on the wet rocks.
items.note: Lose your balance describes failing to remain steady; the possessive changes with the subject.

items.pt: perder o apoio dos pés; escorregar e perder a firmeza
items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: He lost his footing on the icy steps.
items.note: Footing is secure support under your feet, especially on uneven or slippery ground.

items.pt: desviar a conversa de; mudar o rumo da conversa
items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: I tried to steer the conversation away from politics.
items.note: A figurative use of steer meaning deliberately redirect discussion away from a topic.

items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: She took a few steps towards the microphone.
items.note: Take steps describes physical movement here; it can also figuratively mean take action.

items.pt: virar a bicicleta de cabeça para baixo
items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: He turned the bike upside down to inspect the chain.
items.note: Turn something upside down means invert it; take upside down is not grammatical in this use.

items.pt: extraviar-se; perder-se; sair do caminho certo
items.section: C · Changes in speed, movement and direction
items.example: One of the parcels went astray during delivery.
items.note: Go astray can mean become lost in transit; it can also mean deviate from a plan or proper behaviour.

units.title: Unit 48 — Change
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 100–101 (PDF pages 104–105).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Discuss small adjustments and major transformations using appropriate verbs and noun partners.
Use change correctly for seats, jobs, habits, clothes and familiar routines, while distinguishing it from exchange and move house.
Describe new availability, success, improving living standards and emerging problems with natural expressions.
Distinguish intransitive rise and arise from transitive raise to avoid common learner errors.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: We made a few adjustments to the motor settings.
items.note: Make adjustments to something means modify it slightly, often to improve how it works.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: We had to make a slight alteration to the meeting schedule.
items.note: Slight emphasises that the change is small; make, not do, collocates with alteration.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: The developers made a few modifications to the interface.
items.note: A natural pairing for several specific changes, especially in a design or technical system.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: Please make minor adjustments before approving the design.
items.note: Minor stresses that the changes are limited; adjustments are often fine-tuning.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: The team decided to adopt a new approach to fault detection.
items.note: Adopt an approach means begin using a particular method or strategy.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: I had my clothes altered before the wedding.
items.note: Have something altered is a causative pattern: another person usually makes the alterations.

items.pt: abandonar um hábito; romper um hábito
items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: It takes effort to break a habit that has lasted for years.
items.note: Break a habit means stop doing something regularly, often something undesirable.

items.pt: largar o vício; abandonar um hábito
items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: He finally kicked the habit of checking his phone at night.
items.note: An informal expression for stopping a persistent habit, especially an addictive one.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: Automation could revolutionise the way we work in the laboratory.
items.note: Revolutionise the way introduces a radical, far-reaching change rather than a small adjustment.

items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: The historical account describes families who converted to Christianity.
items.note: Convert to names a change of religion or belief; unlike transform, it typically takes to plus the new faith.

items.pt: transformar a maneira como nos sentimos
items.section: A · Ways of talking about change
items.example: A peaceful holiday can transform the way we feel.
items.note: Transform suggests a major change in condition or experience; the unit presents it as potentially positive.

items.example: Could we change places so I can sit near the window?
items.note: Change places refers to swapping physical positions with someone, not exchanging objects.

items.example: The passengers agreed to change seats.
items.note: Change seats means sit in different seats; exchange seats is not normal here.

items.pt: mudar de emprego; trocar de trabalho
items.example: She plans to change jobs after finishing her course.
items.note: Change jobs refers to taking another job; it does not normally mean changing the duties of one job.

items.example: The children had to change schools after the move.
items.note: Use change, rather than exchange, for moving to a different school.

items.example: He decided to change doctors after moving to another city.
items.note: Change doctors means use a different doctor for ongoing care.

items.example: They will move house at the end of the month.
items.note: British English uses move house when changing residence, not change house.

items.example: I changed my mind and booked the earlier train.
items.note: Change your mind means revise a decision, opinion or intention.

items.example: He changed the subject when the conversation became awkward.
items.note: A fixed combination for moving discussion to a different topic.

items.example: We need to change the beds before our guests arrive.
items.note: Here change the beds means replace the sheets or bed linen, not move or buy beds.

items.example: Could you change the baby while I prepare dinner?
items.note: Change the baby is an idiomatic way to say replace the baby’s nappy, especially in British English.

items.example: Please change your clothes before painting the walls.
items.note: Means put on different clothes, not exchange clothes with someone.

items.example: We exchanged money before travelling abroad.
items.note: Exchange money often means convert one currency into another, rather than simply change where money is kept.

items.example: We exchanged addresses so we could stay in touch.
items.note: Exchange addresses means each person gives their address to the other.

items.example: The researchers exchanged ideas after the seminar.
items.note: Exchange ideas means share thoughts or suggestions with other people; change ideas is not equivalent.

items.pt: ficar disponível; passar a estar disponível
items.example: Additional appointments will become available next week.
items.note: Become available describes a change of state; the textbook warns against get available.

items.example: The small business became successful after several difficult years.
items.note: Become successful is the expected pairing for attaining success; get successful is not usual in this context.

items.word: the standard of living is rising
items.pt: o padrão de vida está aumentando; o nível de vida está subindo
items.example: The standard of living is rising in some rural communities.
items.note: The standard of living rises or improves; increasing the standard of living is not the source’s preferred intransitive form.

items.word: the standard of living is improving
items.pt: o padrão de vida está melhorando
items.example: The standard of living is improving as more families gain access to clean water.
items.note: The unit offers is improving as a natural alternative to is rising; it does not use is growing.

items.example: There has been a big improvement in her performance this term.
items.note: Improvement in performance refers to better quality or results, rather than a numerical increase.

items.example: Unexpected problems arise when requirements are unclear.
items.note: Arise is an intransitive verb meaning emerge or occur; its past tense is arose.

items.example: Prices rise when demand grows faster than supply.
items.note: Rise is intransitive: prices rise by themselves; someone raises prices.

items.example: Profits rose after the company reduced its costs.
items.note: Use rise for an upward movement of profits, without a direct object.

items.example: The sun rises earlier in summer than in winter.
items.note: Rise is intransitive here and its past tense is rose; do not confuse it with raise.

items.example: Please raise your hand if you have a question.
items.note: Raise takes a direct object: you raise your hand; your hand rises.

items.example: The government announced plans to raise taxes on luxury goods.
items.note: Raise is transitive and means make something higher; taxes themselves rise.

items.pt: levantar uma questão; fazer uma pergunta
items.example: May I raise a question about the proposed timetable?
items.note: Raise a question introduces an issue for discussion; rise a question is incorrect.

items.pt: levantar um problema; trazer uma questão à discussão
items.example: Several engineers raised an issue during the design review.
items.note: Raise an issue means bring it up for discussion; a common alternative to raise a question.
